rationales: Copper and zinc do not form a coordinate covalent bond when alloyed.
An ionic bond is not the bonding type in brass, which is an alloy of two metals.
Brass is held together by metallic bonding between copper and zinc atoms.
A covalent bond is not the characteristic bond formed between the metals in brass.
Carbon commonly forms covalent bonds but is not the best example of an element forming all three bond types.
Oxygen forms covalent bonds, donates a lone pair in coordinate covalent bonds, and occurs in ionic metal oxides.
Magnesium typically forms ionic or metallic bonds rather than all three types listed.
Silicon commonly forms covalent bonds, but it is not the standard example of an element forming all three types.
The smaller size of oxygen alone does not explain the large difference in boiling points; strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding does.
Water molecules form strong hydrogen bonds, so more energy is needed to separate them than H₂S molecules.
H₂O is lighter than H₂S, but molecular mass does not explain why water is liquid while H₂S is a gas.
Water’s ability to freeze is not the reason it is liquid under ordinary conditions while H₂S is gaseous.
The C–C single bond is relatively strong and is not the weakest of these bonds.
The Cl–Cl bond is considerably stronger than the O–O bond.
The O–O single bond is the weakest listed because repulsion between lone pairs on the two oxygen atoms weakens it.
The F–F bond is weak, but it is slightly stronger than the O–O single bond.
Coal is not the form of carbon commonly used as a lubricant.
Diamond is extremely hard and is not used as a lubricant.
Graphite’s layered structure lets its layers slide over one another, making it useful as a lubricant.
Charcoal is not the form of carbon typically used as a lubricant.
H₂O has the highest boiling point because its molecules form an extensive network of strong hydrogen bonds.
H₂S does not form strong hydrogen bonds, so its intermolecular attractions are weaker than water’s.
HF forms hydrogen bonds, but its boiling point is lower than water’s.
NH₃ forms hydrogen bonds, but they are not sufficient to give it a higher boiling point than water.
Lithium has a higher melting point than the other listed alkali metals.
Sodium has a higher melting point than potassium and rubidium.
Potassium has a higher melting point than rubidium.
Rubidium has the lowest melting point among the listed metals.
NaCl has the highest melting point among these compounds.
KCl melts at a lower temperature than NaCl.
LiCl’s greater covalent character gives it a lower melting point than NaCl.
RbCl has a lower melting point than NaCl.
MgCl₂ is predominantly ionic and does not contain a covalent polyatomic ion.
NH₄Cl contains covalent N–H bonds within NH₄⁺ and an ionic attraction between NH₄⁺ and Cl⁻.
CaO is an ionic compound rather than one containing both ionic and covalent bonds.
PCl₃ contains covalent bonds but no ionic bond.
Ethane contains a carbon–carbon single bond, not a double bond.
Methane contains only single covalent bonds.
Ethylene (ethene) contains a carbon–carbon double covalent bond.
Acetylene (ethyne) contains a carbon–carbon triple bond, not a double bond.
